newsitem.title: USA: Guinness sees year-round growth in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Guinness sees year-round growth in U.S..

text.p: Guinness, renowned for its Irish stout, is expanding its marketing activities in the United States in an effort to spread the appeal of the creamy, dark beer beyond the St. Patrick's Day season.

The brand is sponsoring rare U.S. concert appearances by Irish music legends Van Morrison, Christy Moore and Shane MacGowan, and is conducting its fourth annual "Win Your Own Pub in Ireland" contest, among other promotions.

Guinness also launched its first-ever television advertising in the United States last October, and plans further print and broadcast campaigns this year, said Howard Pulchin, director of communications at Stamford, Conn.-based Guinness Import Co.
Guinness, whose two U.S. brands are Draught Guinness (available on tap and in cans) and Guinness Extra Stout (in bottles), also thinks it has tapped into a growing vogue for all things Irish.

"Irishness is hot and getting hotter," Pulchin told Reuters in an interview. "Irish music is huge these days, literature... and cultural happenings like 'Riverdance' are sweeping the country and the whole world."

The world's best-selling stout has been brewed since 1759 at St. James's Gate Brewery in Dublin. Industry analysts said Guinness has been doing heady business in the United States at a time when overall beer consumption is flat.

"They seem to have found and pushed the right buttons to get this product growing -- it's a consistent grower," said Frank Walters, research director at M. Shanken Communications, publisher of Impact, a beer and wine industry magazine.
Walters said Guinness was growing by 20 percent a year in U.S. volume, against total beer industry growth of one percent, and 10 percent for all imported beers.
Americans consumed about 187 million barrels of beer last year, Walters said.
Guinness sold 5.7 million case equivalents in the United States last year, Pulchin said. He declined to reveal revenues or budgets for marketing and promotion.
"I think Guinness has a bright future in the U.S.," Walters said. "Beer is a mature business. Growth is coming from specialties and imports."
London-based Guinness Brewing Worldwide, the world's seventh-biggest brewer as measured in operating profits, views the United States as one of its fastest-growing markets, Pulchin said.
"St. Patrick's Day season is a popular time for the brand -- sales do go up -- but what we have seen over the past couple of years is that it's big year-round now, it's growing," he said.
Pulchin said Guinness's volume in March last year increased by about 54 percent over every other month.
The brand is now conducting its fourth annual "Win Your Own Pub in Ireland" contest, which has attracted more than 155,000 entries in the past three St. Patrick's Day seasons.

Participants are asked to submit a 50-word essay on the stout in hopes of winning their very own pub in Ireland. Pulchin said the promotion has been extremely successful because it appeals to the imagination.
"There are so many people out there who have a dream of just quitting their jobs, moving to a place like Ireland, running a pub and being part of a quintessential Irish village."
Up for grabs this year is a pub called J. Morrissey's in County Tipperary.
Guinness buys an Irish pub each year before the contest. "We look for a pub with good trade and turnover in a lively town, where someone can move from the U.S. and have a good business."

In an effort to extend the brand's appeal beyond the shamrock season, the company will this June sponsor the first annual Guinness Fleadh (pronounced "flaw," Irish for festival) in New York. The two-day music and arts gala will feature Van Morrison, the Chieftains, Sinead O'Connor, Christy Moore and Shane MacGowan. Also on hand will be Irish-influenced American artists including Natalie Merchant and the band Wilco.
Guinness's advertising and promotions in the United States are handled by public relations firm Cohn & Wolfe and New York ad agency Weiss, Whitten, Stagliano.
